title: Tyagaraja turns down the king
hookLine: a hum before singing, the drone under every note, and a saint who sang to Rama instead of the king
carry: nada upasana: music itself can be worship
tomorrow: someone reads your name off a list wrong. does it really matter?

cards: Before a Carnatic concert begins, before a single word, there's a hum. The tambura, a long-necked instrument, plays one steady drone, and every singer tunes to it.
Try a version now: rest one fingertip on the side of the nose and hum, softly. Feel the buzz, and hold it steady, like that drone.
In South India, about two hundred and fifty years ago, a singer named Tyagaraja gave his whole life to that hum and what grew from it. And one day, a messenger came from the king.

teach.b: The king of Thanjavur had heard him, and, as the story goes, invited him to court with gifts of gold and land. For a poor singer, it was everything. Tyagaraja said no.

He answered in a song still sung today: Nidhi chala sukhama, is wealth the greater joy, or being near Rama? He spent his life singing to Rama, at home, in temples, walking the streets, and left hundreds of songs behind.
In one of them he praises the seven notes themselves. Here's the teaching under the story.
Hindus call it nada upasana, worship through sound. Not music about God, as a show, but singing as the prayer itself. Many Carnatic musicians still begin their practice as an offering.
And every year, at his resting place in Thiruvaiyaru, crowds of musicians gather on the anniversary of his death and sing five of his songs together, as one voice.
Gatherings like it happen around the world, in American cities too.
So when a grandmother hums a bhajan over the stove, or a cousin sings at the temple for nothing, it's the same old road: the voice offered, not sold. The hum you felt in your face is where it starts.

how: Carnatic musicians gather each year at Thiruvaiyaru, and in cities around the world, to sing Tyagaraja's five Pancharatna songs together on the anniversary of his death; many singers begin practice with a prayer and tune to the tambura's drone.

games.why: Tyagaraja chose singing to Rama over a king's gold. nada upasana treats the voice as an offering, not something for sale.

practice: Hum softly on each out-breath, one fingertip on the side of the nose to feel the buzz, as steady as a drone. If you pray, let the hum become one name, Rama or another you love, sung on a single note.
If you don't, just keep the hum. Then let it stop, and feel how the quiet sits in the face.

wordCard.voice: The sounds: today, set to music. Nada upasana, worship through sound, the way Tyagaraja lived it.

orig.note: Sanskrit: nādopāsanā (nāda + upāsanā), worship through sound.
